fr:concept:gender-two-classes.title: Every French noun has a gender
fr:concept:gender-two-classes.shortRule: Every noun is masculine (le) or feminine (la) — the article is part of the word.
fr:concept:gender-two-classes.explanation: French sorts all nouns into two grammatical classes, masculine and feminine. This is a property of the word itself, not of the thing it names, so the reliable way to learn a noun is to learn it together with its article: 'le chat', 'la pomme'. The good news: a noun's ENDING often signals its gender, and the upcoming lessons teach only the ending patterns that a 36,940-noun analysis shows to be genuinely dependable.

examples.note: before a vowel sound the article shortens to l', hiding the gender — eau is feminine

exceptions: Before a vowel sound, both le and la become l', so the article stops showing the gender. For those nouns, remember them with un/une instead: une eau minérale.
